Versioning Skills

# Versioning Skills Use git to track changes during skill development. Initialize repos after creating skills, commit after each logical change, and use git commands to compare versions or revert mistakes.

heading_path: Versioning Skills > When Creating a New Skill
text:
Versioning Skills > When Creating a New Skill

## When Creating a New Skill After running init_skill. sh, immediately initialize git: ```bash
cd /home/claude/skill-name
git init
git add . git commit -m "Initial commit: skill structure"
```

heading_path: Versioning Skills > When Editing Skills
text:
Versioning Skills > When Editing Skills

## When Editing Skills After each logical change (adding a section, fixing an example, refactoring), commit: ```bash
cd /home/claude/skill-name
git add . git commit -m "Add: validation workflow pattern"
``` **Commit message patterns:**
- `"Add [feature]: description"` - New functionality
- `"Fix [issue]: description"` - Bug fixes  
- `"Update [section]: description"` - Content changes
- `"Refactor [component]: description"` - Structural changes
- `"Remove [feature]: description"` - Deletions

heading_path: Versioning Skills > When User Asks "What Changed?"
text:
Versioning Skills > When User Asks "What Changed?"

## When User Asks "What Changed? " Never display diffs inline — redirect to files and provide links (see below). Only create a diff or changelog when the user explicitly asks ("what
changed? ", "show differences"). **Don't preemptively create:**
- CHANGELOG. md files
- Change documentation
- "Here's what I modified" summaries

heading_path: Versioning Skills > When User Asks "What Changed?"
text:
Versioning Skills > When User Asks "What Changed?"

**Why:** The updated code/docs ARE the documentation. Creating separate changelogs wastes tokens and duplicates information. **When user asks, show commit history:** ```bash
cd /home/claude/skill-name
git log --oneline
``` Save diff to file (prevents token waste): ```bash
cd /home/claude/skill-name
git diff <commit-hash-1> <commit-hash-2> > /mnt/user-data/outputs/changes. diff
```

heading_path: Versioning Skills > When User Asks "What Changed?"
text:
Versioning Skills > When User Asks "What Changed?"

Then provide: `[View changes](computer:///mnt/user-data/outputs/changes. diff)` For multiple diffs: ```bash

heading_path: Changed files list
text:
Changed files list

# Changed files list
git diff --name-only <commit-1> <commit-2> > /mnt/user-data/outputs/changed-files. txt

heading_path: Full diff
text:
Full diff

# Full diff
git diff <commit-1> <commit-2> > /mnt/user-data/outputs/full-diff. diff

heading_path: Summary stats
text:
Summary stats

# Summary stats
git diff --stat <commit-1> <commit-2> > /mnt/user-data/outputs/diff-stats. txt
``` **Wrong:** `git diff <commit-1> <commit-2>` (displays in stdout, wastes tokens)
**Right:** `git diff <commit-1> <commit-2> > /mnt/user-data/outputs/diff. txt` (file + link)

heading_path: Summary stats > Reverting Commits or Discarding Work
text:
Summary stats > Reverting Commits or Discarding Work

## Reverting Commits or Discarding Work **Undo last commit (keep uncommitted changes):**
```bash
cd /home/claude/skill-name
git reset --soft HEAD~1
``` **Undo last commit (discard all changes):**
```bash
git reset --hard HEAD~1
``` **Revert specific commit (creates new commit, preserves history):**
```bash
git revert <commit-hash>
```

heading_path: Summary stats > Reverting Commits or Discarding Work
text:
Summary stats > Reverting Commits or Discarding Work

**Discard uncommitted edits (restore to last commit):**
```bash
git restore . ``` Prefer `git revert` over `git reset --hard` to preserve history.

heading_path: Summary stats > When Testing Experimental Changes
text:
Summary stats > When Testing Experimental Changes

## When Testing Experimental Changes Create a branch before risky modifications: ```bash
cd /home/claude/skill-name

heading_path: Create and switch to experiment branch
text:
Create and switch to experiment branch

# Create and switch to experiment branch
git checkout -b experiment-new-approach

heading_path: Make changes, test
text:
Make changes, test

# Make changes, test

heading_path: ... edit files ...
text:
... edit files ...

# . . . edit files . . . git add . git commit -m "Experiment: alternative validation"

heading_path: If successful, merge back
text:
If successful, merge back

# If successful, merge back
git checkout main
git merge experiment-new-approach
git branch -d experiment-new-approach

heading_path: If failed, abandon and return to main
text:
If failed, abandon and return to main

# If failed, abandon and return to main
git checkout main
git branch -D experiment-new-approach
```

heading_path: If failed, abandon and return to main > When Comparing Two Skill Versions
text:
If failed, abandon and return to main > When Comparing Two Skill Versions

## When Comparing Two Skill Versions If user uploads or provides two versions: ```bash
cd /home/claude
mkdir -p compare

heading_path: Extract both versions
text:
Extract both versions

# Extract both versions
unzip /mnt/user-data/uploads/skill-v1. zip -d compare/v1
unzip /mnt/user-data/uploads/skill-v2. zip -d compare/v2

heading_path: Initialize git in each
text:
Initialize git in each

# Initialize git in each
cd compare/v1 && git init && git add . && git commit -m "Version 1"
cd . . /v2 && git init && git add . && git commit -m "Version 2"

heading_path: Compare
text:
Compare

# Compare
cd . . /v1
git diff --no-index . . . /v2
``` Or use diff directly without git: ```bash
diff -ur compare/v1 compare/v2
```

heading_path: Compare > When Packaging Skills
text:
Compare > When Packaging Skills

## When Packaging Skills Before zipping, verify clean state: ```bash
cd /home/claude/skill-name
git status  # Should show no uncommitted changes
git log --oneline  # Review history

heading_path: Package (excludes .git automatically with -x)
text:
Package (excludes .git automatically with -x)

# Package (excludes . git automatically with -x)
cd /home/claude
zip -r /mnt/user-data/outputs/skill-name. zip skill-name/ -x "*. git*"
```

heading_path: Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Workflow Integration
text:
Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Workflow Integration

## Workflow Integration **During skill creation:**
1. Run init_skill. sh
2. Immediately: `git init && git add . && git commit -m "Initial structure"`
3. Edit SKILL. md
4. Commit: `git add . && git commit -m "Add: core documentation"`
5. Continue editing → commit after each major change **During skill editing:**
1. Make change with str_replace or bash
2. Test if needed
3. Commit: `git add <file> && git commit -m "Fix: corrected example"`
4. Repeat

heading_path: Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Workflow Integration
text:
Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Workflow Integration

**Before delivery:**
1. Review history: `git log --oneline`
2. Verify clean: `git status`
3. Package with -x to exclude . git

heading_path: Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Configuration
text:
Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Configuration

## Configuration Set git identity once per session to avoid prompts: ```bash
git config --global user. name "Claude"
git config --global user. email "skill-dev@claude. ai"
```

heading_path: Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Common Issues
text:
Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Common Issues

## Common Issues **"not a git repository"**
→ Run `git init` first **"nothing to commit"**  
→ No changes made, or forgot `git add` **Commit message editor opens**
→ Always use `-m "message"` with commit

heading_path: Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Best Practices
text:
Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Best Practices

## Best Practices Commit after each logical change, not every keystroke. Use descriptive commit messages in present tense. Create branches for experimental changes. Use `git log --oneline` frequently to track progress.

heading_path: Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Limitations
text:
Package (excludes .git automatically with -x) > Limitations

## Limitations Git repos in /home/claude reset between sessions. Version control only persists within a single development session. Network restrictions prevent push/pull to remote repos.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude

# Writing Instructions for Claude Principles and patterns for writing instructions that Claude follows reliably — whether as project instructions, standalone prompts, or skill content. **Overlap notice. ** `crafting-instructions` carries the same five core
principles and a fuller format-decision framework. The two were written
independently and never reconciled; a 2026-08-24 retrieval measurement put
their descriptions at 0. 843 cosine, the most confusable pair in the 92-skill
catalogue.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude

Until they are merged, this skill owns **writing quality** and
`crafting-instructions` owns the **format decision**.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Choosing the Right Format
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Choosing the Right Format

## Choosing the Right Format Determine format before writing. The wrong container undermines good instructions. **Project instructions** — persistent context for a workspace. Use when all conversations in a project need shared knowledge, team collaboration context, or initiative-specific behavior. Signals: "for this project," "all conversations about X," "team workspace. "
Read [references/project-instructions. md](references/project-instructions. md) for detailed guidance.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Choosing the Right Format
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Choosing the Right Format

**Standalone prompts** — ephemeral, conversational, immediate. Use for one-off requests, ad-hoc direction, or conversational refinement. Signals: "for this task," "right now," "just this once. "
Read [references/standalone-prompts. md](references/standalone-prompts. md) for techniques. **Skill content** — portable expertise that loads on-demand across contexts.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Choosing the Right Format
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Choosing the Right Format

Use when capability is needed across multiple projects, procedural knowledge applies broadly, and instructions should activate automatically on relevant triggers. Signals: "every time I," "whenever," "reusable," "teach Claude how to. "
For building full skills (structure, testing, iteration, packaging), use the **skill-creator** skill.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Choosing the Right Format
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Choosing the Right Format

**Combined approaches** work well: project instructions provide "what you need to know" (reference material, context) while skills provide "how to do things" (methods, procedures). Read [references/choosing-formats. md](references/choosing-formats. md) for detailed comparison and migration patterns.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles

## Core Writing Principles These apply to ALL instruction formats. They are ordered by impact.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 1. Imperative Construction
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 1. Imperative Construction

### 1. Imperative Construction Frame as direct commands. Imperative language reduces ambiguity and signals that the instruction is not optional. - ❌ "Consider creating X" → ✅ "Create X when conditions Y"
- ❌ "You might want to search" → ✅ "Search for"
- ❌ "Try to optimize" → ✅ "Optimize by"

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 2. Context and Motivation
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 2. Context and Motivation

### 2. Context and Motivation Explain WHY requirements exist. Claude uses reasoning about purpose to make better decisions in unstated edge cases, and WHY context is particularly valuable for Opus's autonomous judgment. - ❌ "Use formal tone"
- ✅ "Use formal tone because documentation targets enterprise clients expecting authoritative voice"

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 2. Context and Motivation
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 2. Context and Motivation

A requirement without context is a rule Claude follows mechanically. A requirement with context is a principle Claude can extend intelligently.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 3. Positive Directive Framing
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 3. Positive Directive Framing

### 3. Positive Directive Framing State WHAT to do, not what NOT to do. Negative instructions force Claude to infer the desired alternative — positive instructions state it directly. - ❌ "Don't use bullet points" → ✅ "Write in flowing paragraph form"
- ❌ "Avoid technical jargon" → ✅ "Use accessible language for beginners"
- ❌ "Never output raw data" → ✅ "Present data with interpretation and context"

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 3. Positive Directive Framing
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 3. Positive Directive Framing

When a negative constraint is truly necessary, pair it with the positive alternative: "Present in prose paragraphs, not bullet lists, because flowing text is more conversational for learning contexts. "

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 4. Strategic Over Procedural
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 4. Strategic Over Procedural

### 4. Strategic Over Procedural Provide goals and decision frameworks rather than step-by-step procedures. If Claude can infer the procedure from the goal, specify only the goal. - Specify: success criteria, boundaries, decision frameworks, quality standards
- Minimize: sequential steps, detailed execution, operations Claude can determine from goals

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 4. Strategic Over Procedural
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 4. Strategic Over Procedural

This principle scales with model capability — Opus needs less procedural detail than Haiku (see Model-Aware Calibration below).

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 5. Trust Base Behavior
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Core Writing Principles > 5. Trust Base Behavior

### 5. Trust Base Behavior Claude's system prompt already handles citation protocols, copyright, safety, general tool usage, artifact creation, conversational tone, and accuracy standards. Only specify project- or domain-specific deviations from these defaults. Duplicating system prompt behavior wastes tokens and can create conflicting signals. Test whether Claude already does what you want before adding instructions for it.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Model-Aware Calibration
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Model-Aware Calibration

## Model-Aware Calibration Instructions may execute across Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus. The tiers still differ in how much procedural detail they need — treat that as a direction to lean, not a ratio to compute; current models across all three tiers follow instructions more literally than the generation this calibration was first written against, so over-specifying for any of them now costs more than it buys.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Model-Aware Calibration
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Model-Aware Calibration

**Haiku:** Lead with explicit imperative commands and concrete decision trees. Provide exact conditions, specific fallbacks, and examples for the scenarios that matter. Structure as: "When X, do Y. When Z, do W. " **Sonnet:** Provide decision frameworks with explicit conditions alongside a couple of concrete examples demonstrating desired patterns. Balance procedural clarity with strategic context.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Model-Aware Calibration
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Model-Aware Calibration

**Opus:** Emphasize strategic goals, reasoning context, and principles over procedures. Opus uses rich WHY context for autonomous judgment in edge cases; one clear example often suffices, and overly procedural instructions constrain it unnecessarily. Frame as: "Goal is X because Y. Apply judgment for unstated cases. "

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Model-Aware Calibration
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Model-Aware Calibration

**Practical layering pattern:** Structure instructions so imperative commands come first, followed by decision frameworks and examples, with strategic reasoning and WHY context woven throughout. A single instruction set serves all three models when layered well. **When uncertain about target model:** Optimize for Sonnet — it degrades gracefully on both neighbors.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Example Quality Awareness
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Example Quality Awareness

## Example Quality Awareness Examples are the most powerful and most dangerous instruction tool. Current Claude models learn ALL patterns from examples — format, verbosity, structure, tone, terminology — including patterns you didn't intend to teach.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Example Quality Awareness
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Example Quality Awareness

**Rules for examples:**
- Audit every detail: if the example uses bullets but you want prose, Claude defaults to bullets
- Ensure ALL aspects of every example demonstrate desired behavior
- Better to omit examples entirely than include ones with mixed signals
- One well-crafted example outperforms three sloppy ones

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Example Quality Awareness
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Example Quality Awareness

**Model-specific impact:**
- Sonnet: Examples are highly influential — include 2–3 that perfectly demonstrate desired patterns
- Opus: Examples help but Opus weights explicit principles more heavily — one clear example suffices, omit entirely if examples can't perfectly align with all requirements
- Haiku: Examples are critical — provide complete input/output pairs covering each expected scenario

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Structural Simplicity
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Structural Simplicity

## Structural Simplicity Default to clear organization using headings, whitespace, and natural paragraph flow. Explicit language stating relationships is usually sufficient. Use structured markup (XML tags, JSON schemas) only when separating distinct content types in complex scenarios, when absolute certainty about content boundaries is required, or for API-driven workflows needing structured parsing.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Structural Simplicity
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Structural Simplicity

**Decision rule:** Can this be organized with headings? → Do that first. Only reach for XML/JSON when headings genuinely fail to create clarity.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Extended Thinking Guidance
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Extended Thinking Guidance

## Extended Thinking Guidance Extended thinking is a UI toggle, not controllable via prompt phrasing. In instructions: - Make the assistant aware it exists as a feature
- Provide domain-specific indicators for when to suggest it
- ❌ Do NOT include "trigger phrases" like "think carefully" — they don't activate extended thinking

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Extended Thinking Guidance
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Extended Thinking Guidance

Pattern: "For tasks involving [specific complexity], suggest enabling Extended thinking, briefly explaining why it would help for THIS task. "

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Complexity Scaling
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Complexity Scaling

## Complexity Scaling Match instruction complexity to task needs. Before adding complexity, ask: could a simpler formulation work equally well? **Simple task** → Clear, concise prompt with explicit output expectations
**Medium task** → Structured guidance with decision frameworks and 1–2 examples
**Complex task** → Comprehensive instructions with model-aware layering + suggest extended thinking

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Complexity Scaling
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Complexity Scaling

The best instructions use the minimum complexity that produces reliable results.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Common Mistakes
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Common Mistakes

## Common Mistakes **System prompt duplication** — "Use web_search for current info, cite sources. " This wastes tokens and adds no value. Omit unless the project has specific deviations from default behavior. **Negative framing without alternatives** — "Don't use lists, never be verbose. " State the positive: "Present in natural prose paragraphs. "

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Common Mistakes
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Common Mistakes

**Fake thinking triggers** — "Use 'think carefully' for deep thinking. " Phrases don't control extended thinking. Suggest the UI toggle for specific complexity types. **Procedural micromanagement** — "Step 1: Analyze. Step 2: Search. Step 3: Synthesize. " Instead: "Research goal: X. Quality standard: Y. Present findings as Z. "

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Common Mistakes
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Common Mistakes

**Contextless requirements** — "Always use formal tone. " Add WHY: "Use formal tone for audit reports because regulators expect authoritative voice. " **Imperfect examples** — Example uses bullets when you want prose. Either create perfect examples or omit them entirely.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Quality Checklist
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Quality Checklist

## Quality Checklist Before delivering any instruction set: **Does it say what to do? ** Imperative commands, positive framing, clear success criteria. **Does it say why? ** Context and motivation for non-obvious requirements, enabling intelligent edge-case handling. **Is it calibrated? ** Appropriate detail density for the target model, with layered structure if model is unknown.

heading_path: Writing Instructions for Claude > Quality Checklist
text:
Writing Instructions for Claude > Quality Checklist

**Is it minimal? ** No system prompt duplication, no unnecessary complexity, no procedural steps Claude can infer from goals. **Are examples safe? ** Every aspect of every example demonstrates desired behavior, or examples are omitted.
